It's not interested in tricking people. It's interested in other peoples' sorrow and will go to great lengths to torment them by making them do terrible stuff to themselves or others for something they will not get in the end. That's why it's called "a very sadistic cap." It enjoys peoples' pain and misery, and that's its motivation to why it does these things.

item.title: Re: A Very Sadistic Cap [Seeking Greenlight]
item.content:encoded:
Hello Inertia_comrade! lets take a look :)

SAND

+ show block
– hide block

The concept:

Elevator Pitch: My SCP is a cap that can telepathically talk to their victims and tricks them into believing that it's a higher being, and if they do what it demands, they'll be awarded what they truly wanted in life. When the victim completes their task(s), the SCP disappears and leaves them, so they can suffer for what they have done. (So basically, it's a troll)

Overall, the skip doesn't have much context around it, there's no clear motives and no clear in-universe justification for existing. Which as a result, makes the skip feel close to a "thing that does a thing", along with causing it to just feel like your average murder monster.

Another issue I have with this; everything feels very random and disjointed, there's no reason why the skip is a cap, or why the skip specifically has these anomalies (teleportation, telepathy ect.) or why its interested in tricking people. Currently, there isn't any sort of link between these elements, which as result, causes the concept to feel random and a bit overcomplicated.

The narrative:

Central Narrative: In 2010, a man was found dead in his house from suicide. One of his friends went to check on him and saw that the door was unlocked. He decided to enter the house and noticed there were multiple drawings all over the walls and hundreds of pictures in one of the rooms of the SCP. There was also a message on one of the walls that say this,

"I Don't Understand. I Did Everything It Wanted Me To Do, But I Don't Hear It Anymore. I Made It My God. I Pushed Everyone Away From My Life. I Killed My Own Two Kids For It, And Yet It's Abandons Me. I Guess My Fate Wasn't Good Enough…"

First off, this seems much closer to a single incident rather than a narrative. As there's little to no clear arc, and most questions the concept raised are still left unanswered. Along with this, the Foundation doesn't seem to be involved here at all, there isn't anything showing how they found it, what happened during its containment, and what they learnt.- do note that the article is written from their perspective, they wouldn't be able to write an article without mentioning themselves, or what they ended up doing.

As for the narrative itself, it feels like your average murder monster horror story, there's nothing here that really stands out or makes the narrative interesting. The suicide note feels like a narrative device to drum up tension or make the skip seem more dangerous, which (to me at least) comes off as edgy and a bit cliched, considering how much this sort storyline is seen in other media.- on a side note, suicide in general can be a rather sensitive topic, if you do wish to include it, it will need to handled carefully.

Hook:

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The cap can somehow teleport to different places in the world, causing more harm to others. The cap does these things to people because it finds it entertaining.

This if fairly dull, as the skips effects or motives won't be able to carry the article alone, for this to work as a hook (imo), they would need to be integrated and communicated effectively in the narrative (which currently they aren't). Generally speaking, you're looking to put the main idea or core narrative conflict in the hook.

Red or green?
Due to my afore mentioned concerns, no-greenlight.

My recommendations;

- Link all of the concept main elements with each-other, try not to use "somehow" to describe why it has its effects, as it makes the concept feel unfinished/anticlimactic.

-Give the skip a strong motive, show why its like this, and how its end goals/motives affect the narrative.- generally speaking, if you know what the skips end goal is, is much easier to craft a storyline.

- Create a stronger storyline, show more of an arc. Here are some questions you can try building off - how does the Foundation deal with the skip? what do they end up learning? whats the main conflict? who are the characters? how will those characters make me feel? how would I feel by the end of the narrative? whats the main payoff?-what is the narrative building up to?

If you would like me review this (or any concept) further, then please feel free to send me a PM or ask via IRC. Response times generally range from 2-12 hours over PMs. If your looking for additional critiques in general, then I would highly recommend contacting the butterfly squad :)

Cheers,

-RED
